calls.text: {"hypotheses":[{"cause":"Native interop / P/Invoke or CGo call triggering SIGSEGV","detail":"Exit code 139 (SIGSEGV) at the k8s terminated-state level with conf=0.97 is characteristic of a segfault originating in native code called from a managed runtime (.NET P/Invoke, JVM JNI, Go CGo). The managed runtime itself survives but the OS kills the process when the native frame writes to an unmapped address. The consistent crash-loop (BackOff count=7) without OOM evidence rules out memory pressure and points to a deterministic code path — likely a specific message payload or startup routine that always invokes the same native function with an invalid pointer or uninitialized buffer.","anchored_facts":["process_crash","crashloop"],"confidence":0.72},{"cause":"Stack overflow hitting guard page → SIGSEGV on every startup/request","detail":"A SIGSEGV (exit_code=139) can be produced when the thread stack grows into the OS guard page due to deep or infinite recursion. In Go this manifests as a runtime stack-overflow panic that emits SIGSEGV; in .NET/JVM a StackOverflowException can also send SIGSEGV depending on the CLR/JVM version and platform. The deterministic crash-loop pattern (max_restart_count=0 yet BackOff reached 7 events) is consistent with a code path that always recurses to the same depth — e.g., a middleware chain, a proto unmarshalling loop, or a misconfigured retry handler calling itself.","anchored_facts":["process_crash","crashloop"],"confidence":0.55},{"cause":"Heap corruption / use-after-free in unsafe or generated code causing non-deterministic SIGSEGV","detail":"exit_code=139 with SIGSEGV and a high confidence (0.97) from k8s_terminated_state indicates the OS terminated the process on an illegal memory access. In runtimes that allow unsafe blocks (.NET unsafe, Go unsafe.Pointer) or auto-generated serialization code (protobuf, Thrift), a use-after-free or double-free can corrupt the heap allocator's internal metadata. The crash may appear 'random' per invocation but becomes deterministic under the fixed workload the container runs at startup (e.g., loading a config file or replaying a notification queue), explaining why every restart crashes reproducibly within seconds.","anchored_facts":["process_crash","crashloop"],"confidence":0.45}]}

{"hypotheses":[{"cause":"Malformed upstream response payload triggering SIGSEGV in deserialisation code","detail":"An upstream dependency (notification sink, message broker, or webhook target) is returning a structurally unexpected or oversized payload. The notificator's deserialisation or buffer-handling routine dereferences an invalid pointer when the payload doesn't match the expected schema, producing SIGSEGV (exit_code=139). The crash is deterministic per restart because the same bad message is re-consumed from the queue head each time, explaining the tight back-off loop.","anchored_facts":["process_crash","crashloop"],"confidence":0.55},{"cause":"Queue backpressure burst causing concurrent unsafe memory access","detail":"A sudden spike of inbound events from an upstream queue or event stream overwhelms the notificator's concurrency model. A race condition in connection or buffer sharing between goroutines/threads (common in notification fanout paths) causes a write-after-free or null dereference under load, resulting in SIGSEGV. Each restart re-encounters the same load pattern because the queue has not drained.","anchored_facts":["process_crash","crashloop"],"confidence":0.30},{"cause":"Corrupted TLS/connection state from upstream TCP reset causing use-after-free","detail":"An upstream service (e.g., SMTP relay, push gateway, or internal gRPC dependency) is terminating connections abruptly mid-read. If the notificator's connection pool recycles the socket without synchronisation, subsequent reads or writes on the freed connection object trigger SIGSEGV. The crash repeats because the pool is re-initialised on each restart and the upstream continues to reset connections.","anchored_facts":["process_crash","crashloop"],"confidence":0.20}]}

{"hypotheses":[{"cause":"Faulty node memory (hardware ECC error or bad RAM page) corrupting the process address space and triggering SIGSEGV","detail":"Exit code 139 / SIGSEGV with conf=0.97 and persistent BackOff (count=7) suggests the crash is deterministic and not transient. A node with bad RAM pages can silently corrupt mmap'd regions or stack memory, producing a segfault that looks like an application bug but is actually infrastructure-induced. Recommended check: node describe for MemoryPressure/conditions, kernel logs (mcelog/edac), and whether other pods on the same node show similar crashes.","anchored_facts":["process_crash","crashloop"],"confidence":0.45},{"cause":"Container runtime (CRI/kubelet) delivering a corrupted or incomplete rootfs/overlay layer, causing invalid memory access at process startup","detail":"SIGSEGV at startup (max_restart_count=0 yet already 7 BackOff events implies rapid crash-on-start) can occur when the container runtime serves a corrupt overlay mount — the process maps a bad page from its own binary or a shared library and faults immediately. This is a kubelet/CRI-layer issue independent of application logic. Check: crictl inspect on the container, kubelet logs around image pull/unpack, and whether a fresh pull + pod delete resolves the crash.","anchored_facts":["process_crash","crashloop"],"confidence":0.35},{"cause":"Memory-mapped file or volume mount (ConfigMap/Secret/PV) presenting an invalid or zero-length page, causing SIGSEGV on first read","detail":"If notificator mmaps a config file or secret at startup and that mount is truncated or backed by a broken PV, the first read dereferences an unmapped address → SIGSEGV (exit 139). This is a storage-layer issue. Check: kubectl exec (if container stays up briefly) or init-container probe to verify mount contents; PV/PVC status and underlying storage health.","anchored_facts":["process_crash","crashloop"],"confidence":0.25}]}
